memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text:
"'Say to the Israelites: "Anyone who curses their God is to be held
responsible; anyone who blasphemes the name of the LORD is to be put to
death. The entire assembly must stone them. Whether foreigner or
native-born, when they blaspheme the Name, they are to be put to
death"'" - Lev 24:15-16 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
The man in this account had an Egyptian father and an Israelite mother.
It would have been easy for the community to treat him as an outsider —
either to excuse him because he was half-foreign, or to punish him more
harshly for the same reason.

God does neither. The law applied identically, whether foreigner or
native-born.

Dear reader, that principle is more radical than it first appears. In
the ancient world, and often in ours, law bends according to who you
are. Wealth, caste, connections and family name quietly change outcomes.
God's law recognised none of that.

Scripture is consistent on this. Peter said, I now realise how true it
is that God does not show favouritism (Acts 10:34). Paul wrote that
there is no favouritism with God (Rom 2:11). James rebuked a church for
giving the rich man a good seat and the poor man the floor (Jas 2:1-4).

The impartiality of God cuts two ways. It means no one gets special
treatment — and it also means no one is treated as less. The
half-Egyptian man received the same justice as anyone else, which is
itself a form of dignity.

Where do you quietly bend your treatment of people according to their
status? Ask God to make you impartial as He is.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. Do I treat people differently based on status, wealth or background?
2. Have I ever excused wrongdoing because of who did it?
3. How can I show God's impartiality in my home or workplace this week?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text:
Father, You show no favouritism. Root out partiality in me, and help me
treat every person with the same honesty and dignity. Amen.
